en: Homage to the Mother of the Victor (Jinamātā).
[The text begins with] "Right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*), and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Is there not something else possible as well, for the sake of which the mention of the subject matter (*abhidheya*) was made in order to exclude it? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For it is of two kinds," and so forth.
"Body" (*śarīra*) refers to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and the object" (*arthaś ca*) serves as a conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Now, one might ask: "If the body of the treatise (*prakaraṇa-śarīra*) is twofold, then let the purpose (*prayojana*) of both be defined. To this he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*), meaning among those two, namely the word and its denoted meaning.
Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of stating the purpose even for the subject matter? To this he says: "The subject matter," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the arrangement of words" (*śabdasandarbha*), the word "also" (*api*) implies that the "arrangement of meaning" (*arthasandarbha*) is also included.

Regarding the phrase "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth: the connection is that since nothing devoid of a purpose is undertaken for investigation by a discerning person, for that reason [it is stated].
By the sentence beginning with "by this" (NBT 8,2).
This being the case, he shows what the meaning of this sentence is by means of the passage beginning with "because" (NBT 8,2).
"For the sake of its comprehension" (NBT 8,3) means for the sake of the comprehension of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
*iti* means "in this manner. *atra* refers to the sentence beginning with "here" (*atrety ādi*).
NB I s.1: "The accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by right knowledge; therefore, that [right knowledge] is here explained."
NBT 5,1: By the words "preceded by right knowledge" (*samyagjñānapūrvikā*) and so forth, the subject matter and the purpose of this treatise are stated.
NBT-B adds the word *sarva* (all) and reads: "By the words 'preceded by right knowledge, all [activity]' and so forth, [the subject matter and purpose of] this [treatise are stated].
NBT 7,1: For the body of a treatise is twofold: the word (*śabda*) and the meaning (*artha*).
A: The body of the treatise is twofold. P: …[broken]… the body of the treatise.
A: "In that very [place]."
P: broken. I omit *eva* because it does not make sense in this context.
Cf.
NBT 7,2: In this context, the sole purpose of a word is the communication of its own denotation, and nothing else.
Therefore, that [purpose] is not investigated here.
Cf. [the same].
NBT-T: Regarding that, the purpose of the word [is as follows]...
"Now (athā)... [he] says. Quoted by Malvania in footnote 4 on p. 7 of DhPr.
NBT 7,3–4: But if the subject matter were purposeless, then even the composition of words for its comprehension would not be worth undertaking.
[The word] "api" implies that... (as quoted by Malvania in fn.
8 at DhPr p. 7).
See NBTT 4,4: "By the word *api*, the contextual connection of the meaning (*arthasaṃdarbha*) is also included. That [is as follows]."
A: Yes.
P: Broken. NBT 8,1–2: …Therefore, its examination should not be undertaken by a discerning person.
Therefore, by demonstrating that this treatise ought to be commenced, its subject matter and purpose are stated by this [verse].
(The opening statement = NB I.1).
Cf. [the commentary].

*Tātparya* 3b: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) means: because the subject matter (*abhidheya*) is purposeless, it should not be undertaken for examination by a discerning person; therefore [the author says] "of this," and so forth. "Showing" (*darśayatā*) means speaking.
"By this" (*anena*) refers to the initial sentence.
NBT 8,2–3: Since the accomplishment of all human goals is preceded by right knowledge, this [treatise] is commenced for the sake of its comprehension; this is the meaning of the sentence here.
NBT-B: For the purpose of comprehending that.
Cf. [the corresponding passage].
Tātparya 3b: "For the sake of its comprehension" means for the sake of comprehending right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "herein," it refers to the opening statement.

Now, one might object: even if the subject matter and the purpose have been stated, as long as the connection (*sambandha*) and other factors of the treatise are not stated, the engagement of discerning persons (*prekṣāvat*) toward it will not occur. Anticipating this doubt, he says "And herein," and so forth.
Regarding the sentence beginning with "In this [work]," etc.:

although the purpose (*prayojana*) of the subject matter, which is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), is the cause for the accomplishment of all human goals, one might still suspect that this will not serve as a response to what we have stated. Anticipating this, he says: "And in this," etc. Right knowledge is the cause for the accomplishment of all human goals; when this meaning is being expressed, he asks how the connection (*sambandha*) and so forth are thereby stated, and answers with: "For thus," etc.
Since it has been stated that "correct knowledge (samyagjñāna), which is useful for the goals of human life, must be explained," the connection [of the word] is "for that reason" (tasmāt kāraṇāt).

[Objection: But if the opening statement expresses the subject matter and the purpose, why does it not likewise state the relationship and so forth? To this he says: "But not... and so on. [Objection: If it does not state them directly, how then is its presentation capable [of conveying them]? To this he says: "One... and so on.
Dharmakīrti clarifies those [meanings] obtained through implication by means of the words "that" (*tat*) and so forth.
In footnote 1 on p. 9 of *DhPr*, Malvania quotes a similar passage from the *Ṭippaṇī* (sic):
"Now, even if the subject matter and the purpose have been stated... what is the answer? To this he says: "And in this sense... (*asmiṃś cārthe*).

NBT 8,4: And here, the purpose (*prayojana*) of right cognition (*samyagjñāna*), which is the subject matter (*abhidheya*) of this treatise (*prakaraṇa*), has been stated as being the cause for the accomplishment of all human goals.
NBT 9.1: When this matter is being stated, the connection (*sambandha*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the subject matter (*abhidheya*) become stated.
All... stated: Quoted by Malvania in fn.1 at DhPr p. [2].
Malvania omits *punaḥ*.
NBT 10,1f.: "For it has been stated by one who says that correct knowledge (samyagjñāna), which is useful for human goals, is to be explained by this treatise... [that] this is what is meant.
Therefore, [the purpose is] to explain the knowledge of the subject matter...
A: ...in order to produce [such] knowledge.
P: Thus it was said, "and so forth."
A: [The text is] broken.
Malvania: Regarding the initial sentence beginning with *nanu*... he says that [the opponent] does not state it: [This is] quoted by Malvania in footnote 2 at DhPr.
A: What is the connection?
P and Malvania: What is the connection and so forth? NBT 10,4–6:
But this single sentence is not directly capable of stating the connection, the subject matter, and the purpose; rather, by stating one, it shows all three through implication.
He says "yadi... taddarśane" [if... in the perception of that], as quoted by Malvania in footnote 3 on p. 10 of the *Dharmottarapradīpa*.

Cf. *Tātparya* 4a: "If [the cause] is not directly capable, how is it capable? To this he says: "But one... Malvania: "...to this he says 'upon seeing that'... P: "...taddarśa... broken... he says 'one,' etc."
*samarthya-*: A: *samarthataddarśana*... [broken] ... *marthya-*. NB I s.1: ... that is being explained (*vyutpādyate*).
NBT 11,1: The word *tat* is the term for the subject matter (*abhidheya*).

The word *vyutpādyate* is the term for the purpose (*prayojana*). Malvania quotes the following passage from the *Ṭīkā*: "Alternatively, he states the subject matter and the purpose as they are obtained through the force of the *vārttika*" (see fn. 4 at DhPr p. 10).
But surely, since that proficiency is being produced, let it be; what is the point of mentioning the causative suffix (*ṇic*)? To this he says, "The purpose," and so forth.
The meaning is that without the causative suffix, the purpose of the activity of both [the teacher and the student] cannot be obtained.
In that regard, the students acquire proficiency in right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*); the teacher, through the activity of the treatise, employs those who are thus acquiring proficiency.
Thus, when the causative suffix *ṇic* has been applied, this is the form of the causative (*ṇicarūpa*) in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) with respect to the object.
He demonstrates how the purpose of the activity belongs to both [the agent and the object] by means of the passage beginning with "For thus" (*tathā hi*), etc. (NBT 11,3).
Cf. [the relevant commentary].

*Tātparya* 4a: Now, one might object: "It is appropriate to say that its derivation (*vyutpatti*) is being performed; why then is it indicated by means of the causative suffix (*ṇic*)? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states the purpose of indicating it with the causative suffix in the passage beginning with "And the purpose here," etc. Cf. *NBTT* 4,15–16: "Why is it derived? It is indicated by means of the causative suffix."
He states its fruit and the purpose here, beginning with "prayojanaṃ cātra" and so forth.
*NBT* 11,1f.: Here, the purpose is considered for the speaker’s activity of composing the treatise and for the listener’s activity of hearing it.
For indeed, all discerning persons [engage in] an activity [only] because of a purpose...
A: The teacher does not explain that [word].
All A, B, P: This is a form derived from *neyaṇica*.
B8a begins with *neyaṇicarūpam idam*.

[Objection: "Surely, just as the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) have been shown, so too should the relationship (*sambandha*) be shown. To this he says: *sambandha* etc. (NBT 12,1). [Question: "In what way, then, is it to be known? To this he says: *sāmarthyāt* etc. (NBT 12,1). [Question: "How is it to be understood through implication (*sāmarthya*)? To this he says: *prekṣāvatā* etc. (NBT 12,2).

Regarding the phrase "even though they have been stated" (NBT 13,3), the word "even" (*api*) implies that they have also not been stated; this is the meaning. [The author] asks: "In that case, for what purpose are they stated? and replies with the words "in those already mentioned," etc.
(NBT 13,3). [He further asks: "Even if doubt indeed arises, what follows from that? and replies with the words "in the case of doubt," etc. (NBT 13,4).
Now, one might object: "If doubt were a factor for engagement (*pravṛtty-aṅga*), then activity would arise from it. To this he says, "The object," and so forth.
The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that it is not only the ascertainment of the object;
[as stated in] "doubt regarding the non-object" (*anartha-saṃśaya*): the meaning is that it is not only the ascertainment of the non-object.

Therefore, [the meaning of] NBT 14,1 is as follows: "precisely because," that is to say, for the very reason that doubt arises when the aforementioned [conditions] are present. Now, one might object: "Let it be shown how [this applies] to the relationship between the denotatum and so forth. To this he says: (quoted by Malvania in fn. 1 on DhPr p. ...).
A: …as in the case of the purpose of the subject matter.
NBT 12,1f.: However, there is no explicit word indicating the connection; rather, it is to be understood through implication alone.

For by a discerning person, for the purpose of developing correct knowledge... [A]: ...by implication... broken... ...therefore, by implication, it is understood. NBT 13,3–14,1: When a treatise has not been heard, even things that have been stated [in it] are not ascertained.
However, even when the subject matter and so forth have been stated, doubt arises regarding them because they lack a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*); and from doubt, people engage in action.
For even a doubt concerning benefit is a factor for the engagement of discerning persons, while a doubt concerning harm is a factor for their desisting.
For this very reason, the author of the treatise himself [states]...
"In the case of doubt," etc. Now, if [the suffix] were a constituent part of the base (*prakṛti*), ... "In the case of doubt," etc.
Tātparya 5b: Although doubts do indeed arise, [one might ask] how they can be a factor for purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*).
To this he says: "And from doubt," and so forth.
"And because of doubt" (DhPr 13,19).

Regarding the phrase "by the author of the treatise alone" (NBT-T 4,14), [the author] asks: for what purpose is the word "alone" (*eva*) used here? He replies with the words "in the commentary," etc. (NBT 14,2).
If it were thus, the same would apply even to the authors of treatises (*śāstrakṛt*); therefore, he says "In the treatise," and so forth.
"From this" (*ataḥ*) means: because there is neither a purpose nor an inclination for the author of a treatise to state things erroneously, for this reason—this is the meaning.
"In them" (*teṣu*) refers to the subject matter and so forth as stated by the author of the treatise.

[Objection: "Surely doubt arises even regarding things that have not been stated; why then are [the three characteristics] stated for the purpose of producing doubt? To this he says: "Regarding those not stated," and so forth; "impossible," and so forth. *Takṣakacūḍā* is the crest of Takṣaka; the jewel in that is the *takṣakacūḍāratna*; the ornament thereof is the *takṣakacūḍāratnālaṃkāra*. Its *upadeśa*: it is called an *upadeśa* because one is instructed (*upadiśyate*) by means of it; it is a medical statement (*vaidyaka-vacana*). That which exists as equal to that is the *takṣakacūḍālaṃkāropadeśa*.
See *Tātparya* 5b: "By the author of the treatise itself"—the word "itself" (*eva*) excludes the commentators.
*NBT* 14,2f.: For the speech of commentators may be conceived as being otherwise, even for the sake of sport and so forth.

Regarding the authors of treatises (*śāstrakṛt*), we perceive no purpose nor any motivation for their engagement in stating a subject matter (*abhidheya*) and so forth that is contrary [to reality] at the commencement of a work;
therefore, doubt is appropriate in their case.

However, when these are not stated by the authors, it is impossible for listeners to determine whether the work is useless, like a treatise on the art of poetry, or impossible to carry out, like an instruction on adorning the crest-jewel of the serpent Takṣaka with gems to cure fever.
NBT-B2,20: Of the expounders.
NBT-B ibid.: For the sake of sport; A: for the sake of exposition... of the authors of the treatises.
A: [He said: "The activity.
A omits *nā*. A omits *ka takṣaka* and *ta vartata*.
If it is argued, "Let there be this much possibility of a fault; what is the harm?", he says: "In these," and so forth. [Objection:

But even when the subject matter and so on are stated, there might still be non-engagement due to the possibility of it being useless; to this he says: "When they have been stated," and so forth. [Objection:
Even if the possibility of its being useful exists, what follows from that? To this he says: "By that," and so forth.
“*Iti*” here has the sense of “therefore”: the meaning is that because discerning people act on the basis of the possibility of an object, for that reason.
If it is asked, “Let it be so...,” he says:
[The answer is] “refutation” (*dūṣaṇa*) is the possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).

NBT 15,1f.: Among these possible apprehensions of failure (*anarthasambhāvanā*), prudent persons (*prekṣāvant*) do not engage [in an action] even when there is a single apprehension of failure. However, when the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and so forth have been stated, an apprehension of success (*arthasambhāvanā*) arises, which is the opposite of the apprehension of failure. By means of that [apprehension], prudent persons engage [in the action]. Thus, for prudent persons … NBT-B3,2: But when the subject matter and so forth have been stated, [there arises] an apprehension of success—
DhT: *ukteṣu* etc. accords with the reading of NBT-B. However, compare Tātparya 7a: *tataś... evety āha abhidheyādiṣv ityādi*.
Cf.
NBT-T 5,12: "If one speaks of the 'object to be expressed' (vācya) and so forth...
Malvania quotes a similar passage from Ṭīkā.

In footnote 2 on p. 16 of the *Dharmottarapradīpa*: "Now, one might object that even when the subject matter and its expression are present, activity will not occur due to the possibility of the [intended] purpose being absent;
therefore, he says: ... See *Tātparya* 7b:

*iti* has the sense of *tasmāt* (therefore); since discerning persons engage [with a treatise] because of the apprehension of the purpose through those two [subject matter and expression], therefore [the statement of the purpose] is a constituent factor for engagement..."
B and P omit "s.
Malvania quotes from the *Ṭīkā* as follows in footnote 4 on p. 16 of the *Dharmottarapradīpa*: "iti" has the sense of "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

The collective meaning of the opening statement has been stated; now the meaning of its individual parts is being explained by the passage beginning with "non-contradictory" (NBT 17,1). To the question, "What is the lexical meaning of 'non-contradictory'? he says, starting with "in the world" (NBT 17,2).
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "a person who is non-contradictory."
The phrase *tadvat* (likewise) is a refinement of the word *svayam* (itself).
Cf.
NBT-Vi 33,14–18: "That, for its part, is the collective meaning (*samudāyārtha*)."

The meaning of the members (*avayavārtha*) is as follows: since [the treatise] is preceded by right cognition (*samyagjñāna*), it is called "S.1. Here, "right cognition" refers to non-deceptive cognition (*avisamvādaka-jñāna*).
Cf.

DhPr 17,4–5: "Thus, having explained the collective meaning of the sentence beginning with 'right cognition' through this sequence, he now explains the meaning of the individual members starting with 'non-deceptive'."
Cf.
*Tātparya* 7b: "Thus the collective meaning has been shown.
Now the meaning of the individual parts is stated by [the words] 'non-contradictory' (*avisaṃvādaka*) and so forth."
Cf.

NBTT 7,15f.: Having thus explained the purport (*tātparya*) of the sentence as a whole, [the author] says "non-contradictory" (*avisaṃvādaka*) etc., in order to show the meaning of its individual parts. A: [This refers to] the meaning of the collective sense (*samudāyārtha*).
P omits *va avayavā*.
NBT 17,1–3: Correct cognition is non-deceptive cognition.
And in the world, one who causes [a person] to obtain an object previously indicated is called "non-deceptive."
In the same way, knowledge is also called "concordant" when it brings about the attainment of the object itself as it has been revealed [by that knowledge].
(NBT-B3,6 omits *svayam*.
Malvania quotes this from the *Ṭīkā*.)

In footnote 1 on p. 17 of the *Dharmottarapradīpa*: "Now, what is the meaning of the word ‘non-contradictory’ (*avisaṃvādaka*)? To this he says: cf. *Tātparya* 7b: "Furthermore, what is the meaning of ‘non-contradiction’? To this he says: "And in the world," etc.
See DhPr 17,15–16: "Whence, then, does the term 'non-contradictory' apply there? To this he says: "And in the world... (loke ca). [B]:
"Now, the meaning of the word is non-contradictory."

Now, one might object: "Are not the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) distinct as the indicator (*pradarśaka*), the motivator (*pravartaka*), and the obtainer (*prāpaka*)? Therefore, how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such that a cognition which has itself indicated an object is said to 'obtain' it? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says "indicated," etc., in order to establish the identity between the motivator and the obtainer. (NBT 17,3)

Alternatively, some maintain that distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) serve respectively to indicate, to impel toward action, and to bring about attainment with respect to a single object; in order to refute this, [Dharmottara] states "that which has been indicated," etc., demonstrating first the identity between that which impels and that which brings about attainment.

Now, one might object: if the attainment of an object were effected through the medium of activity, then the means of attainment would be subsumed within the impelling one; however, since attainment is established by cognition solely through the medium of its production, he says "for instance," etc.

Nevertheless, there is indeed a distinction between the indicator (*pradarśaka*) and the motivator (*pravartaka*); thus he says [in the *Nyāyabinduṭīkā*], "the state of being a motivator," and so forth.
Now, why is it that the very state of indicating the object of activity (*pravṛttiviṣaya*) constitutes the state of being a motivator? To this he says, "for not... and so forth.
[This is quoted by Malvania in fn. 3 on p. 17 of the *Dharmottarapradīpa*: "Having raised the objection, 'But...,' he says..."]

Or rather... demonstrating their identity, he says. [Malvania omits the following words: "first establishing the identity between the initiator and the obtainer," and "pradarśitetyādi," and "in one and the same object.
All [manuscripts] read: *pradarśitetyādi*.
NBT 17,3f.: "And when the object has been indicated, the very capacity to induce activity is the capacity to cause attainment, and nothing else...
Cf. DhPr 18,3-6: "But surely... and these two functions cannot belong to one and the same [cognition].
For..."
Only P reads *ekasminn evārthe*.
This is written in the margin of P, likely by a different hand. Cf. [source].

Tātparya 7b: The opponent maintains that validity (*prāmāṇya*) belongs to three distinct cognitions regarding a single object, such as "blue," differentiated by their functions as indicating, impelling, and causing attainment. To refute this, [the author] says: "And when the object has been shown," and so forth. Cf. NBTT 8,3–5: Regarding one and the same object, the opponent maintains that validity belongs to three cognitions through the distinction of being indicative, impelling, and attaining; to refute this, he says: "And when the object has been shown."
B,P: showing.
B.
in the gate.
A omits *ḥ prāptiḥ*. P,B: *pravartakeṃtar°*. B: *vidhīyeta*.
A: "By 'knowledge' [it is meant as follows].
NBT 17,3–18,2: For it is not by producing knowledge that [a means] causes one to obtain the object; rather, it causes one to obtain the object by inducing the person to act toward the object.
Furthermore, the state of being an inducer consists precisely in the indication of the object of activity."
For consciousness cannot forcibly impel a person to action.
Cf. NB I sūtras 18–19.
A: Why?
[The word] *eva* and *pravartakatvam* are omitted in A and P.

Regarding "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) and so forth: the meaning is that for this very reason—namely, because the instigator (*pravartaka*) and the obtainer (*prāpaka*) are non-different from the indicator (*pradarśaka*)—it is for that cause.

One might object: "If knowledge fulfills its purpose through mere apprehension alone, then this [distinction between means and result] would indeed be so; but it is not so. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Apprehended," and so forth. If that is indeed the case, what follows from it? To this he replies: "In that way," and so forth. "Precisely for this reason" means that not only is the attainment of the object established as the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) when there is no difference between the indicator and the instigator or the obtainer, but rather, the means of valid cognition itself is established as having for its domain an object not yet apprehended. This is the meaning.

One might object: "Surely, by performing some previously unknown action, the instigator (*pravartaka*) and the bringer-about (*prāpaka*) will become two distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Anticipating this, he says: "By that very [means]... and so forth. NBT 19,1–3: For this very reason, the apprehension of the object itself is the fruit of the means of valid cognition;
for once the object has been apprehended, the person is set in motion, and the object is brought within reach.
And this being so, the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is completed through the apprehension of the object.
For this very reason, a means of valid cognition has as its object that which has not yet been apprehended. (Note: NBT-B3, 10 omits *ca*; A reads *cevam*.)
All: "It is attained," and so forth.
A: Non-difference. P: Established.

A: Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). NBT 19,3–4: For by that very cognition through which an object was first apprehended, the person is impelled toward it and the object is attained. And since [the cognition] occurs with respect to that very [object], a cognition whose object has already been apprehended is not a valid cognition.
NBT-B 3,12 omits *ca*. NBT-B ibid.: *tato*.

It has been stated that "correct cognition is that which makes one attain the object shown"; however, [the author] asks, "In what way, then, does it show that? and says, beginning with *tatra* (NBT 20,1).

Alternatively, having presented right cognition (*samyagjñāna*) in general, [the author] says "In that regard" (*tatra*) and so forth, showing that perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) perform their respective functions in particular.
"In that regard" means between perception and inference; for there is no other right cognition.
"Known as seen" (*dṛṣṭatvena jñātaḥ*) means ascertained (*niścita*).

[Objection: "If [the object] has been seen merely once, why is it not shown by perception itself, such that it is said, 'it is known as something seen'? To this he says, "Because... and so forth (*yasmād ityādi*). [Question:

"How does inference show the object? To this he says, "Inference, however... and so forth (*anumānaṃ tv ityādi*). And this being the case, what [follows]? To this he says, "And thus... and so forth (*tathā cetyādi*).
"Because of this": because they indicate a determined object, therefore they are means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By that [fact], these two alone indicate a determined object;
the meaning is that no other cognition is a means of valid cognition.
In order to support what was stated—that no other cognition is a means of valid cognition—he says, "to attain," and so forth.
To the question, "Even if that is so, what follows from it? he says, "because it brings about attainment," and so forth. Cf. NBT 21,3.
In the same way, cognition (*jñāna*) is also called "concordant" (*saṃvādaka*) when it causes one to attain the object that was itself revealed.
Cf.
*DhPr* 20,6–9: But has it not been shown by this continuous [argument] that valid cognition (*samyagjñāna*) is that which indicates the object of purposeful activity?

According to the principle that will be stated later, there would be no distinction [between them] such that "there are two types of valid cognition (samyagjñāna) called perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna). And thus, it must be explained for whom and how that [distinction] exists; therefore, he says "therein" (tatra).
Cf. [the source].
Tātparya 9a: "And there are two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) according to the method that will be explained.
Now, to the question, "What is the object of engagement for perception and inference? he says "In that regard," and so forth. [The answer is:
"The object (artha)."
All: Regarding this [it is said]:
NBT 20,1–3: "In that context, whatever object is known as being perceived has been made the objective domain of activity by means of perception.

For, in whatever object the operation of perception—its function of direct manifestation—is followed up by conceptualization, perception is the indicator of that [object]; therefore, it is known as being perceived and shown by perception."
Inference, however, having ascertained [the object] through the perception of a logical mark (liṅga), indicates the object of purposeful activity.

If this were the case, because an indeclinable compound would necessarily result in the neuter gender, one could not have such forms as *pratyakṣo ghaṭaḥ* (a perceptible jar) or *pratyakṣā śāṭikā* (a perceptible cloth). To this he says, beginning with "attained" (*prāpta*), etc.: if the word *akṣa* were [inherently] neuter, then since a determinative compound (*tatpuruṣa*) is dominated by its final member, the neuter gender would necessarily apply even to the *tatpuruṣa*. By means of this dependence on the sense-faculties, however, the quality of being a direct perception of the object (*arthasākṣātkāritva*), which inheres in the same substrate as that [dependence], is indicated; that alone is the operational ground of the word.

That which has configuration (*saṃniveśa*)—that is, shape—as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is "that which has configuration as its adjunct" (*saṃniveśopādhi*). Alternatively, the limiting adjuncts of configuration are "adjuncts of configuration" (*saṃniveśopādhayaḥ*); these, together with the phonemes, are the "phonemes that are adjuncts of configuration," and that which has those as its essence is "that which has phonemes that are adjuncts of configuration as its nature" (*saṃniveśopādhivarṇātmaka*).

Now, one might object: "An qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) serves to exclude (*vyavacchedaka*); and here, that which is to be excluded is inference itself, and since that is excluded by just a single qualifier, what is the purpose of employing two qualifiers? For one who acts upon that [perception], a mere tree is obtained; thus, because it is consistent (*saṃvādaka*), it would be correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*), and because it is free from conceptual construction, it would be direct perception—such a doubt might arise. However, that [perception] is not direct perception because it is erroneous (*bhrānta*).
And because it lacks being produced from a logical mark possessing the three characteristics, it is not inference.
Nor is there any other means of valid cognition [to account for it]. (NBT-B:
for the purpose of refuting [this]).

Thus [it is said]. Question: Why does [the text] say "ityādi" (and so forth) instead of "ity āha" (thus he said)? Therefore, what is the purpose of including the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) for the sake of excluding this [type of cognition]?

This is true. However, when this term "non-erroneous" is present, it is understood that perception is a specific kind of cognizing knowledge characterized by correspondence; otherwise, just as inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) merely through correspondence, so too would perception be.

For this very reason, the Vṛttikāra stated (NBT 45,2): "Because one who acts on that basis obtains at least a tree, it would be correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) due to its correspondence (*saṃvādakatva*).
Or, in this context, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) is purposeful.

Some partial followers of the Master [Dharmakīrti] maintain that cognitions such as that of two moons are mental errors (*mānasī bhrānti*) and not sensory; thus, they hold that such errors are excluded by the inclusion of the term "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) alone. Accordingly, they understand that the teacher named Dignāga did not include the term "non-erroneous" in his definition of perception as "perception is free from conceptual construction."

In order to refute their misconception, Dharmakīrti provides the qualification "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) while defining error as that which arises from the sense faculties; thus, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" is faultless. [The objection: But if... [as Dharmakīrti says], the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" is faultless. (p. 18, 16–19, 14) Malvania: *bhrāntagrahaṇaṃ*. (See DhPr pp. 263–264.)

Even though there is no relationship of denoted and denoter (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of an object and a word, nevertheless, it is stated that perception is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) while provisionally accepting this [relationship].

Otherwise, if the relationship of denoted and denoter were to exist with respect to a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, the proof of perception’s non-conceptuality would be entirely pointless; for [perception] does not arise from a universal because its object is the particular characteristic—this is the meaning.

If the relationship between the denoted and the denoter (*vācyavācakabhāva*) is accepted as belonging to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then the intention is that all cognitions would necessarily be conceptual (*savikalpaka*); anticipating this objection, [Dharmottara] says "Even if... (*yady api...*) and so forth.

Therefore, it is not capable of being associated with verbal expression.

Now, he says "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*) and so forth, explaining that the phrase "devoid of that" is connected with the statement "that which is non-erroneous is direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*).

The meaning of "it is shown" (*darśitam*) in the phrase *iti darśitam* (Tātparya 24a) should be understood as "for this reason" (*iti tasmāt arthaḥ*). The ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*) is that [the author] has shown that the two definitions—being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and being non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)—are mutually dependent, and not each individually, by demonstrating that what is devoid of the former and what is non-erroneous constitute the object of the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*). These two definitions, being mutually dependent, are thus shown to have perception as their common referent.
He concludes with the words "iti" and so forth. Since it is thus, therefore [he says].

By stating that "inference is of two kinds," he refutes misconceptions regarding the number of types of inference.
Inference is indeed of two kinds.

It is not threefold as the Naiyāyikas maintain—namely, *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*—nor is it singlefold as the Mīmāṃsakas maintain, who hold that the aforementioned three types of inference are exclusively for one's own sake (*svārthānumāna*) and not for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*). For they argue that the logical mark (*liṅga*) is exactly the same in the inference for others as it is in the inference for oneself; since one utters the logical mark precisely as it exists in the inference for oneself in order to communicate it to another, it remains an inference for oneself. For the Naiyāyikas maintain that there are five kinds of logical mark (*liṅga*), namely: (1) the conjoined, such as smoke, because it is conjoined with fire; (2) the inherent, such as the possession of horns, because it is inherent in the substance "cow"; (3) the inherent in the same object, such as producedness, because producedness and impermanence are both inherent in the same object; (4) the contradictory, such as fire, because fire and cold are contradictory; and (5) the causal, such as the rising of clouds, because it is the cause of the effect, rain. The meaning is that this [fivefold classification] is refuted by one who demonstrates that there are only three types of logical marks.

How so? Conjunction (*saṃyoga*) must not be accepted as an indicator (*gamaka*), because since conjunction resides in both [relata], it would follow that even fire would be an indicator [of smoke]. Furthermore, that which is inherent (*samavāyin*) is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*); and since that which is inherent in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*) is also essentially of the nature of its own being (*svabhāvatva*), and because inherence itself has been refuted; and because that which is contradictory (*virodhin*) is included within non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*); and because a mark that is a cause (*kāraṇaliṅga*) is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Therefore, only three [types of reasons] possess the status of a logical mark (*liṅgatva*). Regarding the passage beginning with "for this very reason" (*ata eva*): since non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is by nature the cessation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), for that reason, non-existence (*abhāva*) is not the object to be proven (*sādhya*).

Now, one might ask: even if non-perception is by nature the cessation of direct perception, from what is it established that non-existence is not the object to be proven? To this he replies: "because of the non-perception of the essential nature" (*svabhāvānupalabdheḥ*).

In this context, the non-perception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is the cognition apprehending the ground as distinct from the jar; it is not the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*) that serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*). Now, an objection is raised: "If the jar is perceptible, how can there be its non-perception? On the other hand, if it is not perceived, how could it be perceptible, such that the cessation of perception is called 'non-perception'? To this, he says: "Even though existing," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "for this reason" (*ataḥ*): the meaning is that even though the jar is not present, it is described as being "perceptible" by virtue of its potentiality when the [ground] associated with the same cognition is appearing; for this reason [it is so stated].

[Objection: Is it not the case that when the ground and so forth—which are conjoined with a single cognition—and that cognition itself are present, it is said that there is the "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) of the perceived jar? "Therefore" (*tasmāt*), and so forth: the meaning is "for that reason," because the cessation of the perceived [jar] is determined from the bare ground and so forth, and from that cognition.
"But not... (*na tu*), and so forth; the word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of "however."

Not only this, but because of the certainty [derived] from the non-perception of the perceptible—namely, from the perceptual certainty grasping the bare ground (kevalabhūtalagrāhipratyakṣaniścayāt)—the absence of the pot (*ghaṭābhāva*), which is the absence of the perceptible (*dṛśyābhāva*), is indeed determined by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), though it has not yet been put into verbal usage (*na vyavahṛtaḥ*), since all sentences possess a restrictive force (*sāvadhāraṇatvāt*).
Anticipating the question, "How, then, is there certainty regarding the non-perception of the perceptible?", he says: "The single... and so forth.

One might object: "If the object is merely suspected to be perceptible, how does this amount to a certainty regarding the non-perception of the perceptible? Then one might further object: "Granted that there is such a certainty regarding the non-perception of the perceptible, yet non-existence would not be certain on that basis alone. To this he says: "yadi hi" (for if), etc.

"From this"—that is, from such a certain non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambhaniścaya*)—there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Now, if the absence of a perceptible jar is indeed determined by the perception that apprehends the bare ground through the non-perception of the perceptible, yet it is not so expressed in conventional usage (*vyavahriyate*), then by what means should it be conventionally expressed? To this he says "the perceptible," and so forth.
The meaning is that it should be conventionally expressed by means of the non-perception of the perceptible, which serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*).

"Therefore" (*tasmāt*) is the conclusion (*nigamana*); the meaning is: because the non-perception of the perceptible—whether in the form of the nature of the bare ground itself or in the form of the cognition grasping the bare ground—is the cause for the ascertainment of the absence of a jar, therefore [it follows].

The meaning is as follows: just as when a floor is being perceived in conjunction with a single cognition, the visibility of a jar—even though it is absent—is superimposed upon it; so too, when that floor has passed away, or is present, or possesses unimpaired memory-impressions, the nature of the jar—consisting of its pastness, presentness, or having unimpaired memory-impressions—should be understood as being superimposed.

Just as the perceptibility of a jar is superimposed upon a perception that is associated with that same single cognition—even though [that perceptibility] does not exist [in the past or future object]—so too should it be understood that the respective forms [of pastness or futurity] are superimposed upon that [object], even though they do not exist, when it is associated with that same single cognition, whether it be in the past (provided the impression for memory is unobscured) or in the present.

Now, when asked by another, "What is the nature of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), at what time is it a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or what is its function?", you stated this sūtra beginning with "unconfused" (*amūḍha*) and so forth, in order to show its nature, time, and function.

Now, fearing that one’s own non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) might likewise be unestablished—just like the non-perception of others which consists merely in the absence of what has been stated and is thus of a trivial nature—he says, “And that,” and so forth.

This is because non-perception, in the form of a cognition apprehending the bare ground, is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), and because the bare ground itself, in its form as the bare ground, is established by the perceptual cognition apprehending the bare ground.
“By that,” and so forth: the meaning is, “by that reason” (*tena kāraṇena*), namely, because it is established.

Regarding the phrase *tataḥ* and so forth: since the past non-perception is clearly a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being remembered, and the present [non-perception] is likewise, for that reason—this is the meaning.

Now, you have accepted that the cognition "it does not exist" arises from non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) alone as its logical mark (*liṅga*); yet this [cognition] is not distinct from the ascertainment of the absence of the jar. A: [the word] "produced-ness" (kṛtakatva).

Now, one might raise the following objection: "If [the absence] is already ascertained by perception alone, then what is the use of non-perception? To this, he provides the answer beginning with "merely" (*kevalam*).

“*Ataḥ*,” etc.: the meaning is that because non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) proceeds toward practical activity (*vyavahāra*) for the sake of determining absence when perception has already performed its function, it is for that reason [that it is so called].
With the word “*iti*” and so forth, he concludes the point previously stated.
“*Anupalambhāt*”: by this reason.

The meaning is as follows: although the ascertainment of non-existence proceeds from the mark (*liṅga*) of non-perception (*anupalambha*) and is known through the intention of another, because it follows the operation of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is produced by direct perception; thus, according to the Teacher’s intention, it is designated and spoken of by means of non-perception in the form of a mark.

That is incorrect, because: in the passage beginning with "nanu ca" (NBT 119,1), when it was objected that just as the ascertainment of existence (*bhāva-niścaya*) arises from the perception of a surface, so too does the linguistic usage of non-existence (*abhāva-vyavahāra*), [Dharmottara] stated by means of the words "kevalam" and so forth that perception itself possesses the capacity for the ascertainment of non-existence, but not the capacity for establishing the linguistic usage of non-existence; thus, it was implicitly stated that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is what establishes the linguistic usage of non-existence. Furthermore, in the passage beginning with "yady api ca" (NBT 122,5), when it was again objected that the cognition "it is not there" arises from the mark (*liṅga*) of the non-apprehension of the perceptible—this alone being the ascertainment of non-existence and nothing else—and therefore the fact that the ascertainment of non-existence is produced by perception and that non-apprehension establishes the linguistic usage of non-existence are not established, [Dharmottara] stated by means of the words "tathāpi" and so forth that, having supported the fact that it is produced by perception, non-apprehension indeed establishes the linguistic usage of non-existence.

"In some cases" means in certain instances, such as: (1) "There is no cold here, because of fire"; (2) "There is no cold here, because of smoke"; (3) "The destruction of an entity that has already come into being is not necessarily certain, because it depends on other causes"; (4) "The causes of cold do not possess unimpeded capacity here, because of the presence of fire"; (5) "There is no falling of frost here, because of the presence of fire"; (6) "He does not have specific symptoms such as horripilation, because of the proximity of a particular fire"; (7) "This place does not contain a person possessed of horripilation and so forth, because of smoke. In these seven types of formal arguments—namely, (1) the perception of what is incompatible with the nature [of the object], (2) the perception of the effect of what is incompatible, (3) the perception of what is pervaded by what is incompatible, (4) the perception of what is incompatible with the effect, (5) the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader, (6) the perception of what is incompatible with the cause, and (7) the perception of the effect of what is incompatible with the cause—the word used expresses a different object (*arthāntara*). (NBT 124,5)

In certain cases—such as (i) "There is no jar here because it is not perceived," (ii) "The causes of smoke, whose capacities are unimpeded in this place, are absent because there is no smoke," (iii) "There is no smoke here because there is no fire," and (iv) "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here because there is no tree"—in these types of applications of the non-perception of essence (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*), the non-perception of effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*), the non-perception of cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), and the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) [NBT 124,5], there is the statement of another negation that serves as the reason for another negation.

This refers to the statement of another essence (*svabhāvāntara*) in the form of a reason, and the statement of another negation in the form of a reason, both being relative to the object to be negated (*pratiṣedhya*).

NB II s.30: And that [negation] is of eleven types due to the difference in its application. NBT 124,5: For a word directly denotes another positive entity in some cases, and in others it denotes another negation.

Now, one might wonder whether this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) in NB 33 is applied to a perceptible *śiṃśapā* tree or to an imperceptible one; anticipating this, he says "this too," etc. (NBT 129,4).

(NB 54). With the words "And this," etc. (NBT 188,10), he states the intended meaning of what was already explained in brief by the word "thus" (evam) and so forth.

The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase *yaś ca* functions as a restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*). [The opponent asks: "Let it be that such a thing is the probandum; what follows from that? To this he replies with the words beginning *yaś ca*.
NBT 188,6f.: "And the established is the opposite of the unestablished."

now, to address the question of what is established if [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhatva*), he says: "As for being unestablished," and so forth.

[One might ask: "How is the meaning characterized by pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, that 'cognition of the contradictory (*viruddha*) does not arise from this because it causes doubt'—understood? And this is the meaning...

Regarding "therefore," etc.: since impermanence and having an origin must be fully known through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that impermanence and having an origin would be established; it is not established in this manner alone. This is the meaning: just as there is no contradiction whatsoever with respect to an effect that is absent simply because its causes are incomplete, so too there is no contradiction whatsoever with respect to an effect whose causes are complete and which is therefore impossible to prevent—this is the meaning.

Now, when light arises in that very same place, what is the explanation? He says, "But when," and so forth. "From that" means: because [the lamp] produces something incapable of darkness and thereby removes it; for that reason.

Now, let it be that the relationship between the removed and the remover exists by way of the relationship between the produced and the producer; however, what is established from this? To this he says, "And therefore," and so forth.

"Yad" means "because. Now, one might ask: "Since even atoms (*paramāṇu*) cannot coexist, why is there no contradiction [in their case]? To this he says, "The continuum," and so forth. (NBT 201,1)
