Now, as for the passage beginning with *yata eva kvacid* (NBT 221,6), one might object that since the statement *yataś ca* and so forth would be redundant if there were no difference [between the two], this is not the case, because it is stated again for the sake of connecting it to the subsequent text; thus, the connection is as follows. Furthermore, regarding what is established from doubt, he says *sandehāc ca*.

(NBT 221,6f.): Precisely because in some cases there is neither certainty of the presence nor certainty of the absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), for that very reason there is doubt regarding positive and negative concomitance.

NBT 221,8f.: If, however, there were a certain determination of the absence of even one of the two—positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—in any instance whatsoever, that itself would be the certain determination of the presence of the second; thus, there would be no doubt at all regarding positive and negative concomitance.
Since there is no certain determination of either presence or absence in any case, for that very reason there is doubt concerning positive and negative concomitance.
And because of this doubt, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
The manuscript A ends with *anvayasya* on folio 83a; folios 83b and 84a are not available to us.
Manuscript P omits the word *śabda*.

P: Why is there a repetition [of the point] regarding "in some cases" (*kvacid api*) concerning positive concomitance (*anvaya*)? To this he says, beginning with "sapakṣa," etc., because there is no certainty regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) and its opposite (*viruddha*) due to the ambiguity of positive and negative concomitance.
The word *hi* here has the sense of "because.

Now, one might ask: "If a third category were possible apart from those things possessing a self (*sātmaka*) and those lacking a self (*anātmaka*), how could there be doubt? To this he says, "And not," and so forth.

There is no repetition of the fault (*punarukta-doṣa*) in stating "and not" and so on, because it serves merely to remind us of the very point already stated in the passage beginning with "for there is no other category besides those possessing a self and those lacking a self."
"From that" means: because there is no other aggregate [of reasons], for that reason.
(NBT 222,3f.): "Of the probandum and its opposite"—because of this, positive and negative concomitance are doubtful due to the absence of certainty.
For when there is doubt regarding the presence or absence [of the reason] in the similar and dissimilar instances, there is no establishment of either the probandum or its opposite.
And no other category besides those possessing a self and lacking a self is possible. Therefore...
[the phrase] "even the non-deviant contradictory" (viruddhāvyabhicārī) means that it is not only [reasons] such as "knowability" (prameyatva) and so forth.
In the phrase "by me, however" (*mayā tu*), the word "however" (*tu*) has the sense of "furthermore.
To the question, "What, then, is the object of inference? he says: "For from which... and so forth.
To the question, "Why, then, is inference possible? he says: "The means of valid cognition... and so forth.

"Why is it that when the three-fold nature [of the reason] is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no possibility of a non-erroneous contradictory [reason]? To this he says: "For when [it is] established by valid cognition," and so forth.
The particle *hi* has the sense of "because.
Now, suspecting that even for a non-erroneous contradictory [reason], its form—that is, its essential nature—might be established by valid cognition, he says: "And not," and so forth.
"From this": because there is no form established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for that reason.
NBT 225,3f.: "The object of inference is the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) established by valid cognition.
For that from which the occurrence of inference arises is the object of inference."

And since inference is possible based on the three characteristics established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), when that [inference] has been set forth, there is no possibility of a "non-erroneous contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).
For when the three characteristics are established by valid cognition...
(NBT 225,6f): Furthermore, for a non-erroneous contradiction, no characteristic is established by valid cognition.
Therefore... [B omits the *ṃ* in *rūpaṃ*.
In the phrase *svabhāvasya ca* (NBT 226,1) and *anupalambhasya ca* (NBT 226,3), the particle *ca* serves as a conjunction.]
Now, as to what was asked regarding the definition of non-perception (*anupalambha*), he says "dṛśya" and so forth.
The phrase "of that too" (*tasyāpi*) means not only of the effect (*kārya*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*).
NBT 226,3f.: And the state of being the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambhatva*) is the definition of non-perception.
Regarding that [inference] as well...
he asks, "Of which inference, then, is scripture the basis? and says, "Scripture," etc.
The word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "not, however" (*na tu*) has the sense of "furthermore."
NBT 226,12: For that inference whose threefold character of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is established by scripture (*āgama*), its basis is scripture.
NBT 227,4: The intention of one who asks "Why? and so forth is as follows:

the meaning of "also" (*api*) is that just as a contradictory non-deviant (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is not possible in an inference proceeding by the force of real entities (*vastubalapravṛtta*), so too it is not possible in one based on scripture.
From what does it arise through error? He says: "For [the cognitions] are inverted," and so forth. [This refers to] the activity of [the senses]. Cf. NB 115b.
“From that” (tataḥ): because the establishment of the state of being a cause exists according to the actual condition of things, for that reason.
But why are they [the causes] such that their existence conforms to the actual condition of things? To this he says: “For those... and so forth.
"From that" means: because they have not been established by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), for that reason.
NBT 227,11f.: "The status of being a reason is not established among reasons through conceptual construction, but rather through the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*). Therefore..."
B,P: *vastunītyādihetutva-*.di is cancelled in P; A: *vastunītyāhetutva-*. Corrected.
NBT 227,13f.: … those [cognitions] which possess such [objects], they are "those whose status is established according to the state of things as they actually exist" (*yathāvasthitavastusthitayaḥ*).
For they stand and are established exactly as things exist, not through conceptual construction;
therefore, in them... [all omit *sthitā*].
Added by us. NBT 227,14: *sthitāḥ*. But the manuscripts [read differently].
C and D read *sthāpitāḥ*.
See DhPr p. 227, n. 12.

Regarding *tena* in NBT 228,5: by that [reason], namely, by that [reason] consisting in the injunction of omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) through the restatement (*anuvāda*) of being connected with [the object] as it exists in all locations; for that reason.
"By that" means by way of being omnipresent.
"And simultaneously"—the word "and" (ca) has the sense of "likewise.
"Therein"—that is, such being the case.
Now, if space were the example, then the two properties previously mentioned would have to exist in space; however, they do not exist, as he says in the passage beginning with "space" (ākāśam).
Having restated that the universal is connected with all locations situated everywhere, its omnipresence (sarvagatatva) is then predicated.
Therefore...

B omits *ta* in *sarvagatatvena*. Anticipating the objection that "it may have the nature of being related to that [object], yet it would not be present in its location," he says, beginning with *yasya* (NBT 229,9). *Tataḥ* means: because whatever has the nature of being related to something must necessarily be present in its location; for that reason.
For that whose nature is related to certain [things], it necessarily exists in their location. Therefore... (A,B:
*san* instead of *tan*).
"‘Ya’ refers to the owner;
‘yatra’ refers to the region of the cow;
and ‘taddeśam’ means the cow belonging to the intended region."

Now, one might object: "Just as an owner who is not present in the region where his cattle are does not pervade those cattle with his own self, so too a universal, being absent from the locations of its relata, does not pervade those relata with its own self. Anticipating this, he says: "In this [context]," and so forth.
"In this" refers to the investigation of the universal.
The word "ca" (and) in the phrase "of those possessing it" (*tadvatām*) serves as a conjunction (*samuccaye*).
Now, he says "And that," etc., [anticipating the objection] that even a relation characterized by inherence (*samavāya*) would apply only to things located in different places.
"By that" means: by that reason through which pervasiveness belongs only to what is not situated in a different place by its own nature.
"Wherein" refers to the individual's own form (*vyaktisvarūpa*); "which" refers to the universal (*sāmānya*); "that" refers to the individual's own form; and "it" refers to the universal.

Now, regarding the location of the inherent form (*samavāyirūpa*), one should establish oneself therein: if the universal were to place its own form in that location, it would not do so by way of encompassing [the individual]. Thus he says, "In that location," and so forth.
"In that location" means in the location of the individual (*vyakti*). "Its encompassing" means the encompassing of the individual.
“From that” means from the placement of its form in that location.
“Inherence in them” means inherence in those individuals; that is *tatsamavāya*. “From that” means from inherence.

"Yat" refers to the universal; "yatra" refers to the individual instance (*vyakti*); "tat" refers to the universal; and "tat" refers to the individual substance (*dravya*). "In its location" means in the location of the individual instance.
[The phrase] "that," etc., refers to those [individuals] mentioned in the passage beginning with "by those situated in all locations," and so forth.
This is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*) that is about to be explained.
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "if it exists" (*asti ca*) has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
Since there is pervasion (*vyāpana*), therefore there is the state of being present in that location (*tad-deśa-sannihitatva*).
"Tad" means: because it is thus, for that reason.
A adds "iti" after "vyāpnoti.
B: [the word] is "ātmānā."
B: Does it pervade?
A, P: No. NBT 230,4f.: That which does not exist in a certain place—that place belongs to it; it does not pervade that place by itself, that is, by its own nature.
In this case, the relationship between the universal and its possessors is characterized by inherence (*samavāya*).
And that [inherence] occurs only between two things occupying the same location.
Therefore, when something is inherent in another, it places itself within the location of its substrate by embracing that [substrate] with its own form.
This very placement within the form of that location is what constitutes the embracing of it; from that, there is inherence in it.

NBT 231,2f.: Therefore, that which is inherent in something pervades that substance and, by its very nature, becomes present in its location. NBT 231,3f.: This is the meaning: ...and there is indeed pervasion;
hence, there is presence in that location.
Thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
By the phrase "by this" (referring to NB 120), it means by the passage beginning with "that which is perceived," and so forth.
"From that" refers to the establishment of the conventional usage of non-existence (*asadvyavahāra*) by way of restating the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*).

Now, [the author] says "of the individual" (*vyakteḥ*) and so forth, because the term "interval between individuals" (*vyaktyantarāla-śabda*) conveys the perception of empty space devoid of individuals; thus, the absence of the universal "cow" in horses and other animals is not established [merely by that].
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and [space] devoid of individuals" (*vyaktiśūnyaṃ ca*) serves as a conjunction (*samuccaye*).

Furthermore, for what reason is it said that by the term "interval between individuals," both another individual and empty space are expressed? To this he says: "even though visible" (*dṛśyam api*) and so forth.

The word *api* has the sense of "because. The particle *ca* in the phrase "and that which was previously mentioned" (NBT 232,4) serves as a conjunction for accumulation (*samuccaya*). The phrase "in a single subject" (*ekasmin dharmiṇi*) refers to the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

But why should there not be a certain conclusion regarding both objects by means of both reasons? To this he says, "For not," and so forth. Now, if the fault expressed by "For not" and so forth were to apply because the two things to be proven are mutually contradictory, and if there were no such mutual contradiction of the things to be proven, he says, "By one," and so forth. "By one" means by the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*).
In the phrase “and in that which is devoid of individuality,” the word *ca* (and) serves as a conjunction (*samuccaya*).
In the phrase “and by another,” the word *ca* has the sense of “furthermore” (*punar-arthe*).
To the objection that existence and non-existence might both belong to a single thing, he says “nor,” and so forth.

"Of one" means of the universal (*sāmānya*); "at one time" means at a single moment; "in one place" means in a single location. "That" means: because existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory, for that reason.

Now, [one might object that] the fault of the "reason characterized by mutual contradiction" (*parasparaviruddhāvyabhicārihetu*) would apply only to the two disciples of Kaṇāda, not to Kaṇāda himself. To this he says, "Since," and so forth.
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "connectedness and visibility" serves as a conjunction.
The word "thence" (*tataḥ*) is in grammatical apposition with "connectedness to all [objects]" and so forth.
It should be understood that the term "pervasion" (*sarvagatatvam*) is likewise accepted [as a reason] in this context.
It should be observed that "non-omnipresence" is also accepted in this case.

The word "therefore" (tataḥ) refers to: [1] its connection with everything; [2] the acceptance of its omnipresence; [3] its perceptibility; [4] the non-perception of it in the intervening space; and [5] the acceptance of its non-omnipresence. Now, one might argue: "If its existence is possible in the case of an object as stated in the scripture, it should likewise be so in the case of a real entity. To this, he says "And not," and so forth.

NBT 231,11f.: By this [statement], having restated the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*), the status of being subject to the conventional usage of non-existence (*asadvyavahāryatva*)—namely, "that [object] does not exist there"—is established. Therefore...
(A,B: *vyaktiḥ* instead of *vyakteḥ*).
NBT 232,1: *vyaktyantarālam*.
However, the manuscripts of NBT A, B, P, and H read *vyakter antarālam*.
See DhPr p. 232, n. 1.
NBT 232,1f.: "The interval between individuals, another individual, and space devoid of individuals.
Even though it is perceptible, the universal 'cow' is not perceived in any particular individual, nor in other individuals such as horses, nor in space devoid of individuals."
B: vyaktāntaraṃsi...
A, P: ? illegible. The manuscript ends around this point.
Folio 86b and folios 87a–b are not available to us.
NBT 232,6f.: "And it is not logical for one [thing] to have both existence and non-existence at one time in one place, because of the contradiction between those two.
Therefore..."

NBT 233,2f.: Since it is accepted that a single universal (sāmānya) is simultaneously connected with [entities] situated in all locations and is also visible, it follows from its connection with everything that it is omnipresent (sarvagata); yet, because it is visible and there is no perception of it in the intervening spaces, it is not omnipresent. Therefore...
B: "In the sense of an unstated conjunction. P: "In the sense of an unstated conjunction.
A: Missing.
NBT 233,5f.: "And its occurrence is not possible in a real entity.

Regarding the two *ca*s in the phrase "and by way of that consequence" (*tatprasaṅgena ca*), they are to be understood as having the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) immediately following [the mention of] "fallacies of the reason" (*hetvābhāsa*) and "fallacies of the example" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).
"That" (*tad*): because examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) and fallacies of examples must be stated by way of that consequence, for that reason (*tasmāt kāraṇāt*).

NBT 233,7f.: But surely, since the reasons (*hetu*) were stated as members of the proof (*sādhanāvayava*), and the fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) followed as a consequence thereof, so too should the examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) be stated as members of the proof, and the fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) follow as a consequence thereof.
That...
NBT 234,3: *Tat* means: because the three-featured reason (*trirūpo hetuḥ*) has been stated, for that reason.
"From this" means from the cognition [of the probandum].
"From that" means: because that very thing is the indicator (*gamaka*), for that reason.

Now, having raised the objection that even if the example lacks the status of being a member of the proof (*sādhanāvayava*), its definition might still be stated separately from the proof itself, he says "And since," and so forth.
"What, then, is being said? he asks with the words "but rather" (*api tu*).
"For this very reason" (*ata eva*) means: for the reason that the example is included within the logical reason (*hetu*), for that cause.
"But not" (*na tu*): the particle *tu* has the sense of "furthermore."
NBT 234,3: It has been stated that the logical reason (hetu) possesses three characteristics; what then is the purpose of the example (dṛṣṭānta)?
NBT 234,4f.: The cognition of the probandum (sādhya) occurs by means of the logical reason itself, which possesses the characteristics already described.
Therefore, that [reason] alone is the indicator (gamaka).

Therefore... the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is not indeed a member (*avayava*) of the proof (*sādhana*). And since it is not a member, the definition of this example is not stated separately from the definition of the reason (*hetu*). NBT 234,7f.: It is not said that the reason exists without an example.
Moreover, the example is not actually included within the reason (*hetu*).
For this very reason it was said:
"Included within the nature of the reason."
"If it is thus" (yady evam) means: if the reason (*hetu*) is not without an example (*adṛṣṭāntaka*), then there must be an example employed for the reason.
Consequently, the definition of that which is employed for the reason must indeed be stated.
This also implies the sense that [the definition] need not be employed for the probandum (*sādhya*).
Now, he says "the example," etc., [in response to the question]: "What is the purpose or the subject matter that would be understood by defining the example?
Anticipating the objection that "in that case, the definition of the example must indeed be stated for the sake of understanding the example," he says "and the example," etc.
"From that" means from the determination of the example based on the definition of the reason (*hetu*).

NBT 235,1f.: "If this is so, then the definition of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) which serves as the basis for the reason (*hetu*) must also be stated. To this he replies: "Because its purpose has already been explained" (s. 151). That is to say, the purpose (*artha*), whether it be the [logical] motive (*prayojana*) or the subject matter (*abhidheya*), of that definition of the example has already been understood. Cf. [NBT 234,8].
NBT 234,7–8 cited above. B:
This is the subject matter (*abhidheya*).
NBT 235,2f.: For the definition of an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is stated so that there may be a comprehension of the example.
And the example is established precisely from the definition of the reason (*hetu*).
Therefore… (B reads *tato* instead of *tarhi*).
B omits *api*.
B: "The example," and so forth.
A omits *hetu*.

B omits *hetulakṣaṇāt*. In the passage from NBT 235,16, *vipakṣāc ca*, the particle *ca* should be understood as having the sense of *eva* (only/just), and it is to be placed immediately after the word *vyāvṛtti*. Now, if the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of the reason has already been stated, for what purpose was the specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) formulated? To this he says: "And not... and so forth.
"From this" (*ataḥ*) means: from that reason because it is not possible to know [it].
"From this" (*ataḥ*) means: for that very reason because it must be stated as being restricted to particulars (*viśeṣaniṣṭha*).
Furthermore, the word "also" (*api*) has the sense of "only" (*eva*); and it is to be understood immediately after "from this" (*ataḥ*).
To the question, "Why is it said that birth (*janman*) must be understood?", he says: "For in birth," and so forth.
The particle *hi* has the sense of "because.
The particle *ca* in the phrase "and from the counter-example" (*vipakṣāc ca*) functions as before.

Now, even if there is an invariable concomitance of the property to be proven (sādhya) with the mere property of the probans (sādhana), nevertheless, identity (*tādātmya*) would not [necessarily] follow; thus he says "tanmātra... and so forth.
Now, when it is stated that the invariable concomitance of the sādhya with that alone must be known, what is established? To this he says "sādhana... and so forth.
In the phrase "and from the vipakṣa," the word "ca" (and) is as before.
The word "that" (tad) is in grammatical apposition with the term "general characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇa). "In this way" (evam) refers to the previously stated reasoning.

"From that" (tataḥ): because the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) must be understood as having such a specific nature, for that reason [it is said]. NBT 235,16f.: "That which is existence only in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), and that which is exclusion from the entire dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)—these two aspects are stated without distinction.
Cf. [the cited passage].
NB III s.122: The nature of the reason has been stated without distinction as its existence only in the similar instances (sapakṣa) and its exclusion from all dissimilar instances (asapakṣa).
… NBT 235,18f.: And even though the general [form] has been stated, it cannot be known; therefore, that very [nature] must be stated as being restricted to the particular.
Therefore, once again, the arising of the effect has been specifically stated as something to be known. For when the arising [of the effect] is known... (NBT 236,2f.):
indeed, the fact that the probans occurs only when that [effect] exists is its identity (*tādātmya*).
Regarding the means of proof...
[NBT 236,5]: Thus, in this way, the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) should be understood as being of the nature of particularity (*viśeṣātmaka*), and not otherwise. Therefore...
A, B: "Co-referential" (*sāmānādhikaraṇaḥ*).
[This refers to] "in this way," by means of the reasoning that is about to be stated.
Now, as for the question of how the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) is to be ascertained, he says: "And the pervasion... and so forth.

Regarding the word "tataḥ" (therefore): because pervasion (*vyāpti*) is ascertained from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the relationship between cause and effect, for that reason [it is said]. Now, where, moreover, is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) to be shown? To this he says, "And that... and so forth. Why is it understood that the negative concomitance is to be shown only in the other case? To this he says, "In the case of fire... and so forth.

The word *hi* has the sense of "because," and the word *ca* has the sense of "therefore": because the cessation of fire is necessarily observed upon the cessation of smoke, therefore that [cessation] must be observed elsewhere than in the kitchen.

Now, since the point is established merely by stating, "Where there is producedness, there is impermanence; where there is an absence of impermanence, there is an absence of producedness," why is it demonstrated with the example of a jar and space? To this he says: "And because of pervasion," and so forth (*vyāpteś ca*, etc.).
Regarding the word *tad*: because of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, for that reason. NBT 236,7f.: ...Thus, the pervasion of the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) has been shown.
And this pervasion is ascertained through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
Then... (NBT 237,1f.):
thus the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) has been shown.
And that must be demonstrated by means of the phrase "as in the other case."

For the cessation of fire must be shown to be invariably concomitant with the cessation of smoke; and that [concomitance] must be shown to exist elsewhere than in the kitchen. (The manuscript ends after "vahninivṛttiḥ").
Folio 88b and the subsequent folios, namely folios 89 and onwards, are not available to us.
B omits *te* in *pradarśitena*. Regarding *anyathā* [in NB 122], it means "without the definition of the particular" (*viśeṣalakṣaṇam antareṇa*).
To the question "Why is it impossible to demonstrate [the particular]? he says, starting with *viśeṣa-* [in NBT 237,9].
The word *ca* [in the phrase] *na ca* has the sense of *tathā* (likewise).

Therefore, the meaning is as follows: just as the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) can be shown without the particular characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), so too can the particular characteristic;
[this applies to] the necessity of its being an effect, and so forth.
"Otherwise" means that it cannot be demonstrated without an example.
In the phrase "and of the essential nature as a logical mark," the word "and" (ca) is used in the sense of conjunction.
In the phrase "and identity" (tādātmyaṃ ca), the word "and" (ca) likewise serves as a conjunction.

Now, while a similar instance (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*) may suffice for demonstrating the means of valid cognition that establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says "vaidharmya... and so forth to address the question: "But for what purpose is the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*)? "Tata eva" (for that very reason) means: for that same reason that the absence of the effect must be shown in the dissimilar instance when there is an absence of the cause.
"Tataḥ" (therefore) means: because the absence of the effect occurs—whether in a real entity (*vastu*) or a non-entity (*avastu*)—when there is an absence of the cause; therefore, for that reason.
The two words "vā" (or) indicate alternative positions.
The phrase beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore) is the concluding statement (*nigamana*).
As for "ataḥ" (hence): because it is impossible to demonstrate either positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) without an example, for that reason.
The word *ca* (and) which occurs [in the text] should be understood immediately after the phrase "that very [word] is to be taken in the sense of 'only'. (NBT 238,9).

Furthermore: "...Therefore, by one who demonstrates the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*), an example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) must be shown.

An example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), however, is for the purpose of understanding the absence of the effect when the cause is absent, provided that the fact of its being an effect is already well-established. (NBT 238,3f.).
Therefore, it is not necessarily a real entity (*vastu*).
Whether in the case of a real entity or a non-entity (*avastu*), the absence of an effect follows from the absence of its cause.
Consequently, both a real entity and a non-entity are accepted as examples by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
B,P: -stacakau. A: missing.
NBT 238,7f.: Therefore, without an example, neither positive concomitance (anvaya) nor negative concomitance (vyatireka) can be demonstrated.
Therefore...
Now, having shown this, he states what is established: "And in this," and so forth.
The word "and" (ca) has the sense of "moreover."
"And the demonstration of cessation"—here, "and" (*ca*) signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*).
"Indeed, only this much"—here, "indeed" (*hi*) has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
"Or for one whose pervasion is well-known"—here, "or" (*vā*) signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Even if the illustration consists of only this much, one might still suspect that although it has been stated, it has not been stated in terms of its substantial reality; anticipating this, he says "And this," and so forth. [B:
in the context of perception.
B omits *caḥ*.]
NBT 239,5: *ca* instead of *vā*; however, the manuscripts A, B, D, P, H, E, and N read *vā*. See DhPr p. 239, n. 6.
Furthermore,
by the phrase "and by this very [same method]," it is stated that not only should the definition of a dissimilar instance (*vyatirikta-dṛṣṭānta*) not be shown, but this is also the intended meaning.
He elaborates on this very point with the words beginning "for thus" (*tathā hi*).
"Even when being appropriated" (*upādīyamāno 'pi*): the word "even" (*api*) implies that let alone when not being appropriated.
[The phrase] "distinct from the manifestation" (*vyaktiriktaṃ*);
[the phrase] "for instance" (*tathāhi*), etc.

[Objection: If these examples have been presented, they will then serve as the means of proving the probandum (*sādhyasādhaka*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "And these... and so forth; "not-all... and so forth.
He says "not all," etc., because atoms will not possess the characteristic of having a physical form (*mūrtilakṣaṇa*).
Then he says "but they are eternal," etc., because they will not possess permanence.
"From that" means: from that reason, namely, because they are asserted to be eternal.
In the phrase "but the jar" (*ghaṭas tv iti*), the particle *tu* has the sense of "moreover.
NBT 240,5f.: "...these examples have been presented.
And these are the faults of the example... because atoms possess corporeality (*mūrtatvāt*)."
Matter (*mūrti*) is the dimension of a substance that is not all-pervading.
Atoms are both non-all-pervading and substantial in nature;
furthermore, they are held by the Vaiśeṣikas to be eternal.
Therefore, it is not devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
As for the jar...
[After "ete ca" etc., B repeats the following: "Even when it is being employed," meaning that let alone when it is not being employed.
Anticipating the objection that "if these examples are presented, they will then serve as the means of proving the thesis," he says: "And these... and so forth.
[Then] "Now, all... and so forth. He says:
"Everything," and so forth.
*Tataḥ* ("therefore") is omitted in manuscripts B and P;
it has been added by us.

Now, [the author] says "But the probandum... (*sādhyaṃ tu* etc. because even the probandum might be doubtful in the case of a man on the street. Furthermore, he says "both of those as well" (*tadubhayam api*) because both non-omniscience (as the probandum) and the possession of passion and so forth (as the reason) would be free from doubt in the case of a man on the street. [In the example: "The means of proof is doubtful in the case of a man on the street, which serves as the instance. (*rathyāpuruṣe dṛṣṭānte sandigdhaṃ sādhanam*).
But the probandum (sādhya) is the certain state of being subject to death;
"not omniscient" means that non-omniscience is the probandum.
The reason is "because of possessing passion and so forth.
Both of these [reasons] are doubtful in the example of the man on the street (*rathyāpuruṣa*).
(B reads *tadvitayaṃ* instead of *tadubhayaṃ*.)
What then is it that is not seen? He says: "But not...
(*na tu*). [The phrase] "even though existing" (*vidyamāno 'pi*)—here the particle *api* has the sense of "although.
[The phrase] "from that" (*tataḥ*) is a positive injunction of possessing passion and so forth, following upon the restatement of the property of being a speaker.
"By that" means by rule.
"The respondent as well, and the proponent as well"—the word "as well" (*api*) is used in the sense of conjunction.
"By that": by that reason, by which both the proponent and the respondent are grasped by the term "desirable" (*iṣṭa*).
If only the mere existence [of the reason] is established, what then remains unestablished? To this he says: "But the pervasion," and so forth.
"By that" means: by that reason because the pervasion is not established.
NBT 241,12f.: "The one who speaks"—having restated the state of being a speaker (*vaktṛtva*), the possession of passion and so forth (*rāgādimattva*) is predicated.
Therefore, there is a necessary restriction of the property of being a speaker with respect to having passion and so forth; by this, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is stated.

Regarding the phrase "like an accepted person" (*iṣṭapuruṣavat*), by the use of the term "accepted," both the opponent (*prativādin*) and the proponent (*vādin*) are included. Thus, the mere existence of the properties of being a speaker and having passion and so forth is established in the accepted person.
But pervasion is not established; therefore... [P adds *ti* to *api*, reading: *apīti*. P:
Is it *asiddhatvāt*?]
B: broken.
A: missing.

Now, since properties such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*) exist in the example of a jar and so forth, how could there be an "unshown positive concomitance" (*apradarśitānvaya*)? To this, he says: "In this [world]," and so on. (NBT 242,1)
The word "here" (*iha*) refers to the formal application (*prayoga*). The particle "also" (*api*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), meaning "even by way of impermanence.
"Over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*) consists in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the property] being cookable and so forth.

If the cognition of the probandum does not arise merely by seeing a similarity such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), how then does it occur? To this he says, "But if," and so forth. Regarding the passage beginning with "Therefore," etc.: because when "being produced" is known to have "impermanence" as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the cognition of the probandum occurs; for that reason. Now, suspecting that even this [reason] might be one where the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has not been demonstrated, he says, "And that," etc.

Now, if the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of a jar and so forth has been demonstrated when stating that "being produced" is invariably concomitant with "impermanence," then this example of the jar would not be one where the positive concomitance is undemonstrated; thus he says, "But by this..."—that is, by the speaker.
Then, [anticipating the objection] that even if it is presented in this way, it might still be useful, he says, "And such as this..."
Now, [the author] says "na ca" and so forth, [anticipating the objection]: "The proof of the probandum (sādhya) will occur even from mere similarity (sādharmya) alone. "Ataḥ" means:
for this reason, because the proof of the probandum is not effected by that which is useful merely as a similarity; therefore, for that cause.
Then, [the author] says "tadarthaś ca" and so forth, [anticipating the thought]: "Perhaps this too would be shown as the meaning of positive concomitance (anvaya)."
"For that purpose" means for the sake of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
To the question, "What is its nature as shown by this [definition]? he says "sādharmya... and so forth.
This is because of the reason stated in the *Nyāyabinduṭīkā* (NBT) 243,1.
But how is it that this [reason] is faulty due to a defect in the speaker? To this he says "vaktṛ" and so forth.
The particle *hi* has the sense of "because.
"Here" refers to the inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
If it is indeed the case that another must be instructed, then why [is this so]? To this he says: "Therefore" (*tataḥ*).
(NBT 241,16f.): ... "Because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) is the reason (*hetu*).
In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), "like a jar," the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has not been demonstrated.

In this case, although sound is similar to a jar by virtue of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), it cannot nevertheless be understood as similar [to the jar] even by virtue of impermanence (*anityatva*), because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). However, if it is known that the state of being produced has impermanence as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then from the state of being produced there can be the cognition of impermanence.
And that [example] is precisely one in which the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has already been demonstrated.
However, by this [method], the example is presented without even stating the sentence of positive concomitance;
and such [an example] is useful solely by way of similarity (*sādharmya*).
Furthermore, the probandum is not established through similarity alone.
Therefore, the example is intended for the purpose of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), yet that purpose has not been achieved by this [example].
Moreover, the purpose of similarity has been introduced but is useless; thus, due to the fault of the speaker, this constitutes a fault of the example.
For in this case, the opponent is the one who must be made to understand.
Therefore... B: impermanence...
Because: [P omits *ta*.
B? broken.]
The manuscript B ends at folio 74b with *nāma* or its vicinity; folio 75ab of B is not available to us.

[The author] says "And if it were so" (*evam ca*) in NBT 243,5, meaning: "If it were thus shown that being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is necessarily concomitant (*niyata*) with impermanence (*anityatva*), then the proof of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*) would occur."

Now, he asks: "In this presented example, what is shown to be restricted where? and answers: "But here... Then he asks: "In that case, what kind of 'producedness' (kṛtakatva) is shown? and answers: "But producedness...
"From that" means from producedness.

Just as impermanence alone is shown to be necessarily concomitant with being produced, but being produced is not [shown to be necessarily concomitant] with impermanence, he demonstrates this with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and so forth.
The phrase "therefore" (*ataḥ*) refers to the prescription of "being produced" by way of restating "impermanence. The word "not" (*na tu*) means "not at all."
Regarding the word *tataḥ*: because it has been shown that being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is not necessarily concomitant with impermanence (*anityatva*), for that reason.

Now, if being produced is in fact necessarily concomitant with impermanence, why is it said here that "being produced was shown to be non-necessary with respect to impermanence"? To this he says: "Even though... and so forth.
Regarding the word *ataḥ*: because it was shown by the speaker to be non-necessary, for that reason.
"From that" means: because the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is defective due to a fault of the speaker and not in itself, for that reason.
"Even a reversed concomitance" (*viparītānvaya*) means that it is not only a case of unshown concomitance (*apradarśitānvaya*); this is the meaning of the word "even.

Now, if it is argued that it is only appropriate to consider the example as defective due to its own inherent fault, and not as defective due to a fault of the speaker, he says "for the sake of others," etc.
NBT 243,5f.: In the example, it must be shown that being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is invariably concomitant with impermanence (*anityatva*).
In this way, there would be a cognition of impermanence from the state of being produced.
However, in this case [of the reason], impermanence is shown to be invariably concomitant with the state of being produced.
But being produced is not necessarily restricted to impermanence;
therefore,
[the other property] is restricted.
P omits ṃ. A and B: missing.
And thus.

Therefore, it is stated that being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is necessarily concomitant with impermanence (*anityatva*), but impermanence is not necessarily concomitant with being produced.
Although, according to the actual state of things, being produced is indeed necessarily concomitant with impermanence, nevertheless, it was shown by the speaker to be non-necessary.
Consequently, although it is itself faultless, it becomes faulty due to the fault of the speaker.
Therefore, even the reversed positive concomitance... and in inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), the fault of the speaker is also considered.
In the phrase "also by way of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyeṇāpi*), the particle *api* has the sense of "furthermore."

"And because of formlessness" (*amūrtatvāt*): the word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction. Now, one might wonder: does "excess of means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇātiśaya*) mean an abundance of measures, or an excellence of the means of valid cognition such as perception and so forth, or perhaps something else entirely? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The means of valid cognition... and so on.

Furthermore, [one might argue] that Kapila and others could be omniscient or authoritative persons (*āpta*), yet they would not be teachers of the science of astrology; to this he says: "If indeed... and so on.
In the phrase "na ca," the particle *ca* has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).

In "anāptatāyāś ca," the particle *ca* serves as a conjunction (*samuccaye*). In "jyotirjñānaṃ ca asarvajñaś ca," the *ca*s serve as conjunctions; likewise, in "āptā vā," the *vā* and *ca* serve the purpose of conjunction (*samuccayārthe*).

NBT 245,15f.: "The excellence of the means of valid cognition" (pramāṇātiśaya) intended here refers to the teaching of astrology (*jyotirjñāna*). For if Kapila and others were omniscient or authoritative persons (*āpta*), why did they not teach astrology and the like?
And it is not the case that...
P omits *caḥ*. Added by us. NBT 246,2f.:
For [if it were so], he would teach astrology and yet be either non-omniscient or untrustworthy.
P reads *vāś* instead of *vā*.
P omits *cca*.
Regarding the phrase *trayīvidā hi* at NBT 247,12, the particle *hi* has the sense of *yasmāt* (because).
"And those free from passion" (*vītarāgāś ca*): the particle *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*).
To the question, "How is the cessation of the probans—namely, the state of possessing passion and so forth—doubtful? he says: "Even though," and so forth.
(P omits *hi*).
P omits *caḥ*. Added by us.
NBT 247,13f.: The exclusion of the proof of possessing passion and so forth from Gautama and others is doubtful.
Although...
"and" (*ca*) [in the phrase] *svīkṛtaṃ ca* indicates a conjunction (*samuccaya*).
[In the phrase] *parigrahāgrahayogasya ca*, the "and" (*ca*) indicates a conjunction (*samuccaya*).
To the question, "Why is the exclusion of both [possibilities] doubtful?", he says: "In the case of Ṛṣabha," and so forth. The particle *hi* has the sense of "because.

The particle *api* in "even the connection with possession and non-possession" (*parigrahāgrahayogo 'pi*); the particle *ca* in "and being free from passion" (*vītarāgatvaṃ ca*); the particle *ca* in "and those who are free from passion" (*vītarāgāś ca*); and the particle *ca* in "and those who are without possessions" (*niḥparigrahāś ca*)—all of these serve as conjunctions (*samuccaye*).
"And it is accepted.
This is not identified in the *Nyāyabinduṭīkā*.

NBT 248,6: They do not relinquish what has been accepted. NBT-T 212,13f: Because they do not abandon what has been taken as their own. NBT 248,8–10: Based on this example of the bull and so forth, the cessation of the probandum (*sādhya*), namely the state of being free from passion, and of the probans (*sādhana*), namely the connection with acceptance and non-acceptance, is doubtful.
Cf. [the relevant passage].

NBT-T 213,2f.: There is doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), namely the state of not being free from passion, and the means of proof (*sādhana*), namely the examples such as the bull and so forth, which consist in the exclusion (*nivṛtti*) [of those qualities].
NBT 248,9: *nivṛttiḥ* is used instead of *vyāvṛttiḥ*, though the manuscripts [read the latter].
C, E: exclusion (vyāvṛttiḥ). See Malvania, p. 248, n. 3. NBT-T: exclusion (ldog pa).

If, indeed, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*), would there still be a fault in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for that reason alone? To this he says: "And of this," and so forth.
"That" (*tat*) has the sense of "therefore.
[NBT 249,10f.: By that [pervasion], negative concomitance is not established.
And to establish this point, there is an illustration.
[The text says: "That...

even if indeed the meaning is understood from another in the case of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), nevertheless, what does that matter in the present context? To this he says: "Even though pure," and so forth. (NBT 250,3)
The word "yadi" (if) connects with "ataḥ" (therefore) regarding the meaning that is about to be stated.
Now, [the opponent] might argue that even if it is not made manifest, the example could still be the cause for establishing the probandum; to this, he says "prakāśita" and so forth.
The particle "api" in the phrase "syād api" (it might also be) expresses a possibility.

Now, anticipating the objection that the example of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) and the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) might establish the probandum even by merely demonstrating similarity and dissimilarity, he says "And not," and so forth.
If the understanding of the probandum does not arise from similarity and dissimilarity, then how does it arise? To this he says "But rather.
"Therefore" means: because the understanding of the probandum arises only from a reason that is necessarily concomitant with the probandum, for that reason.
"From that" (*tasmāt*) means: because the reason, which is restricted to the probandum (*sādhyaniyata*), must be demonstrated by means of an example; for that reason.

Now, one might think that this [statement] too would merely demonstrate dissimilarity (*asādṛśya*) and thus demonstrate the meaning of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*); therefore he says "nor... (*na ca*), and so forth. "From this" (*ataḥ*) means: from the fact that the statement of negative concomitance has not been employed; for that reason.
Now, [the author] says "na ca" and so forth, [anticipating the objection]: "It will be a means of proof even by mere similarity.
"Tathā" means "by mere dissimilarity.
To the question, "In what way, then, is it a means of proof?", he says "vyatireka" and so forth.

Now, one might ask: why has this [reason] not been presented as having the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as its object, such that it would not be a prover? To this he says, "And not," and so forth. "In that way" means by way of having the negative concomitance as its object.
"Thus" indicates the reason.
NBT 250,3f.: In this case of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), the object must be understood from another.
Even if that [object] is pure in itself, if it is represented as impure by another, then that [impurity]... is what is revealed as the reason (*hetu*).
Therefore, even due to a fault of the speaker, the reason or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) may be defective in an inference for the sake of others.
The realization of the probandum does not arise from similarity or dissimilarity, but rather from a reason that is invariably concomitant with the probandum.
Therefore... that [reason] which has been stated must be shown as established by means of an example.
Consequently, what is called an "example" (dṛṣṭānta) is the demonstration of the meaning of the statements regarding positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
Furthermore, no statement of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) has been employed here.
Therefore, the example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) presented here is intended as a proof merely by way of non-similarity;
yet it is not a proof in that manner.

It is a prover by virtue of having negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as its object, yet it has not been presented in that manner... [text partially broken] ...it would not be a reason (*hetu*). Therefore, [it is not a valid reason].
B: *vyatireka-* instead of *vyatireka-*.
[The phrase] "even by mere dissimilarity" (*bathāsadṛśyamātreṇāpi*).
Now, if the reason (*hetu*) restricted to the probandum (*sādhyaniyata*) must be shown, then why does he say "and when," etc. (*yadā ca* etc.)? (NBT 252,1)

Why must the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) be shown as being necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probans (*sādhanābhāva*)? To this he says: "For in this way," and so forth. Now, if the absence of the probandum were shown as not necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probans, what would be the fault? To this he says: "But if," and so forth. If the absence of the probandum were even possible when the probans is present, what would be the fault? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.
"Therefore" means: for this reason, because it is so.

Now, [the author] says "if the contrary," etc., [anticipating the objection]: "Even if the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not inverted, could it not be shown that the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is necessarily restricted to the absence of the probans (*sādhanābhāve*)? He clarifies this very point with the words "for instance," and so forth.
"From that" (*tataḥ*): because the affirmation of the absence of the probandum follows upon the restatement of the absence of the probans;

for that reason. And what would happen in this case? To this he says, "And thus," etc. "From that" (*tataḥ*): because it has been stated that the property of being unproduced (*akṛtakatva*) is necessarily concomitant with permanence; for that reason.
To the question, "What is the intended meaning [of this]?", he says: "And thus," and so forth.

NBT 252,1f.: Here, by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the logical reason must be shown to be necessarily restricted to the probandum (*sādhya*). And when [the reason] is necessarily restricted to the probandum... the absence of the probandum must be shown to be necessarily restricted to the absence of the probans (*sādhana*).

For such is the nature of the reason... if, however, the absence of the probandum were not stated as being necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probans, then the absence of the probandum might be suspected to occur even when the probans is present.
Therefore, the absence of the probandum must be stated as being necessarily concomitant with the absence of the probans.
And in the case of a reversed negative concomitance, [the reason] is non-conclusive with respect to existence.

"May I be engaged in the welfare of the world"—having attained what state? What kind of state? "Undecaying" (*ajara*), and furthermore, of what nature? "Surpassing knowledge and virtue" (*jñānadharmottara*), meaning preeminent or primary through both knowledge and virtue; or else, that state in which knowledge and virtue are the two preeminent factors is "surpassing knowledge and virtue. For what reason, having attained that state? "From this merit" (*ataḥ kuśalāt*)—that merit which was obtained or acquired by me. Of what nature is this merit? "Stainless" (*amala*), meaning pure. Like what? "Like rays" (*aṃśuvat*), like beams. Of what? "Of the moon" (*indoḥ*). By what means was this merit obtained? "By the commentary on a few words" (*katipayapadavyākhyayā*). Of which work? Of the treatise *Nyāyabindu*. Such is the meaning of the verse.

By whatever stainless merit I have acquired through this brief commentary on a few words and topics of the *Nyāyabindu*—having attained the undecaying state of Jñānadharmottara, which is like a ray of the moon—may I, being solely occupied with the welfare of the world, [attain] it.
